title: Binary data in Node.js: encodings, byte order, and shared memory
description: How `Buffer`, `Uint8Array`, `ArrayBuffer`, and `DataView` relate, how encodings and byte order work, which operations share memory, and why turning binary data into a string destroys it. We ran every code sample in Node to check the answers.

questions.title: `Buffer` is a subclass of which built-in JavaScript typed array?
questions.description: Name the standard typed array that Node's `Buffer` extends. Every Buffer is also an instance of it.

images.alt: A box for Uint8Array, the standard built-in, with an arrow labeled extends pointing up to it from a box for Buffer. Buffer is the Node global that adds readInt32BE, write, and toString('hex'). A note says buf instanceof Uint8Array is true, but the reverse is not. Below, brackets mark one six-byte region twice: buf covers all six bytes, and buf.subarray(0, 2) covers the first two. A note says a write through either reference shows up in the other. Two cards sort operations by what they do. buf.subarray and Buffer.from(arrayBuffer) share the same bytes, while Buffer.concat and new Uint8Array(buf) allocate new memory and copy.
images.caption: The arrow points to the class Buffer extends.

questions.explanation:
`Buffer` is a subclass of `Uint8Array`, the standard byte array. You can check it yourself:

```js
Buffer.from([1, 2, 3]) instanceof Uint8Array;                      // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Buffer.prototype) === Uint8Array.prototype;  // true
```

The relationship goes one way. Every Buffer is a Uint8Array, but a plain Uint8Array is not a Buffer (`new Uint8Array(1) instanceof Buffer` is `false`). Because a Buffer is a Uint8Array, you can pass one to any standard API that takes a Uint8Array, such as `TextDecoder`, Web Crypto, or a `fetch` body. Buffer adds Node conveniences on top: string encodings, fixed-width integer reads like `readInt32BE`, `toString('hex')`, and an allocation pool.

questions.title: What is an `ArrayBuffer`, and how do you read the bytes inside it?
questions.description: You write `const ab = new ArrayBuffer(8)`. How do you get at the individual bytes?

images.alt: An ArrayBuffer of eight bytes, 00 00 00 01 01 00 00 00, drawn as eight cells. Beneath it, a Uint8Array view has eight one-byte elements, and a Uint32Array view has two elements of four bytes each. Two cards read the same bytes both ways. Bytes 0 to 3 give 1 with readUInt32BE and 16,777,216 with readUInt32LE, and bytes 4 to 7 give the reverse. A closing note says endianness is only the order in which a view assembles bytes, and that four bytes per element is why new Uint32Array(4).byteLength is 16.
images.caption: The top row has no accessors of its own. The rows beneath it are the views.

options.text: It is a fixed-length block of raw memory with no element accessors. You read it through a *view*, such as a `TypedArray` or `DataView`.
It is an array of bytes, so you index it directly with `ab[0]`.
It is a growable list of numbers, so you call `ab.push(byte)` to append data.
It is a UTF-8 string buffer, so you call `ab.toString()` to read its contents.

questions.explanation:
An `ArrayBuffer` is a fixed-size chunk of raw memory. It has no way to read or write its contents directly: `ab[0]` is `undefined`, and there is no `.push`. To reach the bytes, wrap the buffer in a *view*:

```js
const ab = new ArrayBuffer(8);
ab[0];                         // undefined — no element access
const bytes = new Uint8Array(ab); // a view over the same 8 bytes
bytes[0] = 255;                // now you can read and write
new DataView(ab).getUint8(0);  // 255 — a different view of the same memory
```

This split is the core of JavaScript's binary model. One `ArrayBuffer` owns the memory, and any number of views (`Uint8Array`, `Float64Array`, `DataView`) can read that same memory in different ways. A Node `Buffer` is one of these views: a `Uint8Array` with extra methods.

questions.title: What is `new Uint32Array(4).byteLength`?
questions.description: The array holds four 32-bit unsigned integers. How many *bytes* does it take up?

images.alt: An ArrayBuffer of eight bytes, 00 00 00 01 01 00 00 00, drawn as eight cells. Beneath it, a Uint8Array view has eight one-byte elements, and a Uint32Array view has two elements of four bytes each. Two cards read the same bytes both ways. Bytes 0 to 3 give 1 with readUInt32BE and 16,777,216 with readUInt32LE, and bytes 4 to 7 give the reverse. A closing note says endianness is only the order in which a view assembles bytes, and that four bytes per element is why new Uint32Array(4).byteLength is 16.
images.caption: Every Uint32Array element takes four bytes.

questions.explanation:
`length` counts elements, and `byteLength` counts bytes. A `Uint32Array` stores 4-byte integers, so 4 elements take 4 × 4 = **16 bytes**.

```js
const a = new Uint32Array(4);
a.length;                      // 4  (elements)
a.byteLength;                  // 16 (bytes)
Uint32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT; // 4
```

That is why the view type matters. The same 16-byte `ArrayBuffer` holds 16 elements as a `Uint8Array`, 8 as a `Uint16Array`, 4 as a `Uint32Array`, and 2 as a `Float64Array`. For a Node `Buffer`, which is a `Uint8Array`, `length` and `byteLength` are always equal because every element is one byte.

questions.title: Which statements about `Buffer` versus `Uint8Array` are correct?
questions.description: Select every true statement about how Node's `Buffer` relates to the standard `Uint8Array`.

images.alt: A box for Uint8Array, the standard built-in, with an arrow labeled extends pointing up to it from a box for Buffer. Buffer is the Node global that adds readInt32BE, write, and toString('hex'). A note says buf instanceof Uint8Array is true, but the reverse is not. Below, brackets mark one six-byte region twice: buf covers all six bytes, and buf.subarray(0, 2) covers the first two. A note says a write through either reference shows up in the other. Two cards sort operations by what they do. buf.subarray and Buffer.from(arrayBuffer) share the same bytes, while Buffer.concat and new Uint8Array(buf) allocate new memory and copy.
images.caption: `instanceof` holds in one direction only.

options.text: `Buffer` extends `Uint8Array`, so `buf instanceof Uint8Array` is `true`, and a Buffer works anywhere a Uint8Array does.
`Buffer` adds methods that a plain `Uint8Array` lacks, such as `readInt32BE`, `write`, and `toString('hex')`.
`Buffer` is a Node.js global. `Uint8Array` is a standard JavaScript built-in that browsers have too.
A plain `Uint8Array` is an instance of `Buffer`, so `new Uint8Array(8) instanceof Buffer` is `true`.

questions.explanation:
The first three are true. The subclass relationship runs in one direction only:

```js
Buffer.from([1]) instanceof Uint8Array;  // true  (Buffer is a Uint8Array)
new Uint8Array(1) instanceof Buffer;     // false (but not the reverse)
typeof Uint8Array.prototype.readInt32BE; // 'undefined' — a Buffer-only method
Buffer.from([1, 2, 3]).toString('hex');  // '010203'
new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]).toString();    // '1,2,3' — inherited Array-style join
```

Think of `Buffer` as `Uint8Array` plus Node conveniences: string encodings, fixed-width integer reads and writes, and an internal allocation pool. In code that runs in both Node and the browser, use a plain `Uint8Array`. Reach for `Buffer` when you need its encoding and number helpers.

questions.title: How many bytes is the string `café` in UTF-8?
questions.description: Give the result of `Buffer.byteLength('café', 'utf8')`. Count bytes, not characters.

images.alt: The string café drawn as four character cells above five UTF-8 byte cells: 63, 61, 66, and C3 A9 for é. So Buffer.byteLength('café', 'utf8') is 5. A dashed line then splits the stream between C3 and A9. Chunk one decodes to 'caf' plus a replacement character, and chunk two decodes to a replacement character alone. A green card gives the fix: join the bytes with Buffer.concat, or decode with StringDecoder. An orange card notes that data += chunk does the same thing to every chunk of a binary file, turning invalid bytes into replacement characters that cannot be turned back.
images.caption: Four characters, five bytes.

questions.explanation:
`c`, `a`, and `f` take one byte each in UTF-8, but `é` (U+00E9) takes two (`0xC3 0xA9`). The total is **5 bytes**, although the string has only 4 characters.

```js
'café'.length;                     // 4  (UTF-16 code units / characters)
Buffer.byteLength('café', 'utf8'); // 5  (bytes on the wire)
Buffer.from('café').toString('hex'); // '636166c3a9'
```

Many bugs come from mixing up character count and byte count. A `Content-Length` header, a fixed-size buffer, or a substring offset computed from `.length` will be wrong for non-ASCII text. When you need bytes, measure them with `Buffer.byteLength`, not `String.length`.

questions.title: What does `Buffer.from('SGVsbG8=', 'base64').toString('utf8')` return?
questions.description: Decode the Base64 text `SGVsbG8=` to a UTF-8 string and type the result.
questions.explanation:
`Buffer` converts between encodings. The Base64 text `SGVsbG8=` decodes to five bytes, `48 65 6c 6c 6f`, which are the ASCII codes for `Hello`.

```js
Buffer.from('SGVsbG8=', 'base64').toString('utf8'); // 'Hello'
Buffer.from('Hello').toString('base64');            // 'SGVsbG8=' (round-trip)
Buffer.from('Hello').toString('hex');               // '48656c6c6f'
```

The pattern is always the same: `Buffer.from(input, fromEncoding)` turns text into bytes, and `.toString(toEncoding)` turns the bytes back into text. Supported encodings include `utf8`, `hex`, `base64`, `base64url`, `latin1`, and `ascii`. The Buffer holds the actual value. The two strings are just different ways of writing the same bytes.

questions.title: You read a binary file with `let data = ''` and `stream.on('data', c => data += c)`. Why is the result corrupted?
questions.description: You collect raw binary chunks into a string with `+=` instead of keeping them as Buffers. What goes wrong?

images.alt: The string café drawn as four character cells above five UTF-8 byte cells: 63, 61, 66, and C3 A9 for é. So Buffer.byteLength('café', 'utf8') is 5. A dashed line then splits the stream between C3 and A9. Chunk one decodes to 'caf' plus a replacement character, and chunk two decodes to a replacement character alone. A green card gives the fix: join the bytes with Buffer.concat, or decode with StringDecoder. An orange card notes that data += chunk does the same thing to every chunk of a binary file, turning invalid bytes into replacement characters that cannot be turned back.
images.caption: Every chunk goes through the same lossy decode.

options.text: `data += chunk` decodes each Buffer as UTF-8. Bytes that are not valid UTF-8 become the replacement character `�`, and that loss cannot be undone.
String concatenation is too slow, so chunks arrive faster than they can be appended and some get dropped.
`+=` keeps only the last chunk because strings are immutable, so each chunk overwrites the one before.
The bytes are fine in memory. The data only looks wrong when printed, because the terminal cannot display binary.

questions.title: Decoding a UTF-8 stream with `chunk.toString()` on each chunk sometimes produces `�`. Why?
questions.description: You decode each chunk separately and join the strings. A multi-byte character can fall right on a chunk boundary.

images.alt: The string café drawn as four character cells above five UTF-8 byte cells: 63, 61, 66, and C3 A9 for é. So Buffer.byteLength('café', 'utf8') is 5. A dashed line then splits the stream between C3 and A9. Chunk one decodes to 'caf' plus a replacement character, and chunk two decodes to a replacement character alone. A green card gives the fix: join the bytes with Buffer.concat, or decode with StringDecoder. An orange card notes that data += chunk does the same thing to every chunk of a binary file, turning invalid bytes into replacement characters that cannot be turned back.
images.caption: The dashed line falls inside `é`.

options.text: A multi-byte character can be split across two chunks. Neither half is valid UTF-8 alone, so each decodes to `�`. Join the *bytes* first, or use `StringDecoder`.
`toString()` randomly fails on long inputs, so some characters get lost.
`Buffer.toString()` does not support UTF-8, so you must pass `'utf16'` to avoid `�`.
The stream delivers chunks out of order, which scrambles the characters.

questions.explanation:
A stream splits data by byte count and ignores character boundaries. The euro sign `€` is three bytes, `e2 82 ac`. If one chunk ends after `e2 82` and the next starts with `ac`, decoding each chunk separately gives two invalid fragments:

```js
const euro = Buffer.from('€');      // <Buffer e2 82 ac>
const c1 = euro.subarray(0, 2);     // e2 82  (incomplete sequence)
const c2 = euro.subarray(2);        // ac     (orphan continuation byte)
c1.toString() + c2.toString();      // '��'  — corrupted, each half is invalid
Buffer.concat([c1, c2]).toString(); // '€'   — join the bytes, then decode once
```

There are two correct fixes. You can collect the raw chunks and decode once at the end with `Buffer.concat`. Or you can use Node's `string_decoder`, which holds back an incomplete sequence at the end of a chunk until the rest arrives:

```js
const { StringDecoder } = require('node:string_decoder');
const d = new StringDecoder('utf8');
d.write(c1); // ''   — withholds the partial character
d.write(c2); // '€'  — completes it on the next chunk
```

questions.title: What is `[...new Uint8Array([256, -1, 300])]`?
questions.description: A `Uint8Array` holds bytes from 0 to 255. What happens to initial values outside that range?

options.text: `[0, 255, 44]`. Each value is taken modulo 256, so only the low 8 bits are kept.
`[255, 0, 255]`. Values are clamped to the range 0 to 255.
`[256, -1, 300]`. The numbers are stored unchanged.
It throws a `RangeError` because the values do not fit in a byte.

questions.explanation:
A `Uint8Array` keeps only the low 8 bits of each value it stores. It wraps modulo 256 instead of clamping or throwing:

```js
[...new Uint8Array([256, -1, 300])]; // [0, 255, 44]
// 256 % 256 = 0,  -1 wraps to 255,  300 % 256 = 44
Buffer.from([257])[0];               // 1  — Buffer is a Uint8Array, same rule
```

If you want clamping, where negatives become 0 and anything above 255 becomes 255, use `Uint8ClampedArray`. The Canvas API uses it for pixel data:

```js
[...new Uint8ClampedArray([256, -1, 300])]; // [255, 0, 255]
```

Knowing which rule applies saves you from bugs where a computed byte silently wraps around instead of raising an error.

questions.title: Read as a 32-bit integer, the bytes `00 00 00 01` give `1` one way and `16777216` the other. What causes the difference?
questions.description: The same four bytes produce two different numbers. What decides which one you get?

images.alt: An ArrayBuffer of eight bytes, 00 00 00 01 01 00 00 00, drawn as eight cells. Beneath it, a Uint8Array view has eight one-byte elements, and a Uint32Array view has two elements of four bytes each. Two cards read the same bytes both ways. Bytes 0 to 3 give 1 with readUInt32BE and 16,777,216 with readUInt32LE, and bytes 4 to 7 give the reverse. A closing note says endianness is only the order in which a view assembles bytes, and that four bytes per element is why new Uint32Array(4).byteLength is 16.
images.caption: The same four bytes, assembled in two orders.

options.text: Byte order, or endianness. Big-endian reads `00 00 00 01` as `1`, and little-endian reads it as `0x01000000`, which is `16777216`.
Signedness. One reading treats the bytes as signed and the other as unsigned.
Number base. One result is hexadecimal and the other is decimal.
A misread. `16777216` means the four bytes were misaligned in memory.

questions.explanation:
A multi-byte integer can store its most significant byte first (big-endian) or its least significant byte first (little-endian). So the same bytes encode different numbers:

```js
const buf = Buffer.from([0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x01]);
buf.readUInt32BE(0); // 1         — 0x00000001
buf.readUInt32LE(0); // 16777216  — 0x01000000
```

For external data, `DataView` is safer than a plain `Uint32Array`. `DataView` makes you state the byte order, while a `Uint32Array` silently uses the CPU's order, which is little-endian on x86 and ARM:

```js
const ab = Uint8Array.of(0, 0, 0, 1).buffer;
new DataView(ab).getUint32(0);       // 1        (big-endian is the default)
new DataView(ab).getUint32(0, true); // 16777216 (littleEndian = true)
new Uint32Array(ab)[0];              // 16777216 (whatever the CPU uses)
```

Network protocols and many binary file formats are big-endian, which is why big-endian is also called network byte order. Decode them with an explicit big-endian reader like `readUInt32BE` instead of trusting the platform default.

questions.title: Which of these operations return something that *shares* memory with the source instead of copying it?
questions.description: Shared memory means a write through one reference shows up through the other. Select every operation that shares.

images.alt: A box for Uint8Array, the standard built-in, with an arrow labeled extends pointing up to it from a box for Buffer. Buffer is the Node global that adds readInt32BE, write, and toString('hex'). A note says buf instanceof Uint8Array is true, but the reverse is not. Below, brackets mark one six-byte region twice: buf covers all six bytes, and buf.subarray(0, 2) covers the first two. A note says a write through either reference shows up in the other. Two cards sort operations by what they do. buf.subarray and Buffer.from(arrayBuffer) share the same bytes, while Buffer.concat and new Uint8Array(buf) allocate new memory and copy.
images.caption: Two brackets over one region, and two cards that sort sharing from copying.

options.text: `buf.subarray(0, 2)`. It is a view onto the same bytes, so writing to it changes `buf`.
`Buffer.from(arrayBuffer)`. It wraps the existing `ArrayBuffer` in place without copying.
`Buffer.concat([a, b])`. Its result stays linked to `a` and `b`.
`new Uint8Array(buf)`. Its result stays linked to `buf`.

questions.title: What is the difference between `Buffer.alloc(1024)` and `Buffer.allocUnsafe(1024)`?
questions.description: Both create a 1 KB Buffer. One is faster, and one is safe to read right away. Which is which, and why?

options.text: `alloc` fills the memory with zeros. `allocUnsafe` skips that step for speed, so it may expose leftover bytes from memory used earlier.
`allocUnsafe` memory can be freed manually, while `alloc` memory is garbage-collected. The names are about memory management.
`allocUnsafe` may throw when memory is low, and `alloc` never throws.
`alloc` creates a fixed-size Buffer, and `allocUnsafe` creates one that can grow.

questions.explanation:
Both return a 1024-byte Buffer. `Buffer.alloc` fills it with zeros first. `Buffer.allocUnsafe` hands you memory, often from a pool, without clearing it, so it can still hold old bytes, including data from elsewhere in your process:

```js
Buffer.alloc(8).toString('hex'); // '0000000000000000' — always zeroed
Buffer.allocUnsafe(8);           // e.g. <Buffer a0 3f 00 ...> — leftover bytes
```

That is what makes it unsafe. It is faster because it skips the fill and may reuse Node's internal memory pool. But if you send or save the buffer before overwriting every byte, you can leak sensitive data. Default to `Buffer.alloc`. Use `allocUnsafe` only when you will overwrite the whole buffer right away, for example when reading into it from a file or socket.
